short_definition: Hedonic adaptation is the tendency for people to return to a fairly stable level of happiness after positive or negative changes, so new purchases and upgrades quickly feel normal.
explanation: Hedonic adaptation, also called the hedonic treadmill, is why the thrill of a new phone, a bigger home or a pay rise fades. The new thing becomes your normal, and your expectations rise to match it. The same process can help people adjust to setbacks over time, although some major life events can affect happiness for much longer.

Hedonic adaptation matters for both happiness and money. If each upgrade only gives a temporary boost, chasing the next one can lead to lifestyle inflation, where spending rises with every raise and savings don't. Knowing this helps you tell spending that genuinely improves your life from spending that just resets your expectations.

Common ways to counter it include spacing out treats instead of making them permanent, spending on experiences and relationships you value, practising gratitude, and deliberately keeping some fixed costs low after a raise. The aim isn't to deny yourself everything. It's to choose upgrades on purpose rather than by default.
example: Example (illustrative numbers): Jordan buys a 900 phone and feels thrilled for a few weeks, but by month three it feels ordinary. Replacing it every year would cost 900 a year, while keeping each phone for three years costs about 300 a year. Jordan chooses the three-year cycle and automatically moves the 600-a-year difference into savings.
common_mistake: Believing the next purchase, promotion or income level will finally bring lasting satisfaction, and permanently raising fixed costs to get there.
title: Hedonic Adaptation
